newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Food drives S.African inflation to 16-month high.
newsitem.headline: Food drives S.African inflation to 16-month high.

text.p: Sharply higher food costs drove South African consumer inflation to its highest level since June 1995, at 9.1 percent year-on-year, the Central Statistical Service said on Wednesday.
Increases in the price indices for food contributed 0.5 percentage point to the overall 1.0 percent month-on-month increase in the consumer price index last month.
That lifted the annual rate of increase for food prices to 12.4 percent in October, two percentage points higher than the 10.4 percent recorded in September.
The data disappointed South African markets which had been hoping for an annual CPI rate below nine percent.
A Reuters consensus poll of economists had forecast a 0.7 percent month-on-month increase and an 8.8 percent year-on-year rise.
"The general consensus was it would hold under nine percent and we'd go to nine percent or higher in November," said Mike Brown, chief economist at stockbroker Frankel Pollak.
"Now we've got there a month earlier (and) November looks as though it will be around 9.3, or perhaps even high."

The fact that such a large proportion of October's increase was due to food prices provided some consolation, however, since seasonal factors are expected to brake recent steep food price increases in the coming months.
Food prices have been caused by shortages of some winter crops due to unseasonal rain, notably vegetables where prices surged 11 percent month-on-month in October.
The summer crop position is expected to be better, helped by better supply and lower international grain prices. The increase in meat prices should also start to slow down, economists said.
Most economists expect South African inflation to peak in November, or possibly December, plateauing around nine percent in the first half of 1997.

South Africa's consumer inflation rate sank to a 24-year low of 5.5 percent last April but has been climbing since in reaction to the sharp fall in the rand which has lost around 30 percent of its value against the U.S. dollar since February.

Of the 0.5 percentage point month-on-month increase in October's CPI not attributable to food price increases, the CCS said 0.1 percentage point was down to higher transport costs and 0.4 percentage point to other constituents of the index.
